reports.name: Pete Crow-Armstrong
reports.published_report: The .516 xSLG sits at the 98th percentile, and the 13.6% barrel rate backs it up — this is a genuine plus-power profile wearing a center fielder's jersey. What makes the current Statcast line interesting is the gap between that raw damage (.378 xwOBA, 96th percentile) and a 25.9% strikeout rate that barely clears the bottom fifth of the league. He chases at 34.4%, which is the friction point: the power and the walk rate (11.4%) coexist with real contact volatility, and the whole profile rides on whether he can hold that chase rate from bleeding higher as pitchers get deeper looks. If the discipline holds, the projection's .948 OPS and 46 home runs across 728 plate appearances is a realistic destination; if the chase rate creeps up, the strikeouts follow and the batting average erodes well below what the xBA of .266 suggests. The 29.5 ft/s sprint speed at the 96th percentile adds 39 projected steals to a power line that would already make him one of the more valuable outfielders in the NL.

reports.name: Junior Caminero
reports.published_report: The contact quality here is almost unfair for a 23-year-old: 92.8 mph average exit velocity, a 13.3% barrel rate, nearly half his batted balls classified as hard-hit. That profile explains why ValuCast projects 44 home runs in a full season, and the .896 OPS doesn't require any luck to sustain, given an xSLG of .499 and an xwOBA of .363 off current Statcast data. The discipline numbers are quietly doing real work too, an 11.2% walk rate against an 18.4% strikeout rate that leaves him in net-positive territory most hitters never reach at his age. The one thing that could limit the ceiling is the defense — an OAA percentile sitting at 1 means he may have to move off third base, and if that happens, the offensive bar for his position goes up considerably.

reports.name: Elly De La Cruz
reports.published_report: The contact quality is almost absurdly good, and the strikeout rate is the only thing separating him from a perennial MVP conversation. A 94.8 mph average exit velocity with a 16.5% barrel rate puts him in elite company for raw damage, and the expected numbers back it: .378 xwOBA, .511 xSLG, neither of which are outrunning the Statcast profile. The 27.3% strikeout rate is the lever, and if he presses that down even modestly, the projection's .881 OPS with 30 home runs and 28 steals becomes a floor rather than a ceiling. Everything here points toward a middle-of-the-order force; a 10.8% walk rate says the strike zone feel is already developing, the legs show up at 28.4 ft/s sprint speed, and at 24 years old the strikeout number is the one variable left with room to move.

reports.name: Jackson Merrill
reports.published_report: The power contact combination is legitimate: a 12.6% barrel rate and 49.3% hard-hit rate translate into an .xSLG of .494, and the projection's 27 home runs alongside 27 stolen bases follow naturally from 91.5 mph average exit velocity and 29.0 ft/s sprint speed. What keeps the ceiling from climbing further is the plate discipline, a 36.9% chase rate that sits at the 14th percentile and a 6.2% walk rate to match, and that's the one lever that would move this profile from very good to genuinely dangerous. reports.name: Jordan Walker
reports.published_report: The contact metrics and the exit data don't point in the same direction, and that tension is the whole Walker profile. His 92.5 mph average exit velocity and 13.2% barrel rate are genuine top-tier contact quality, and an xSLG of .468 lines up cleanly with the projection's .479 SLG across a full 671 PA season. The problem is a 35.7% chase rate and 31.9% whiff rate that sit near the bottom of the league, and those numbers explain why his xBA (.268) lags so far behind what the raw power suggests he should be hitting. If pitchers keep attacking him out of the zone and he keeps biting, the strikeout rate (25.5%) eats into the counting stats and the .335 OBP projection is probably the ceiling, not a floor. The sprint speed (29.1 ft/s) keeps the 21-steal projection honest and adds a floor of base-running value even if the swing decisions don't improve, but this is fundamentally a contact-discipline story: if the chase rate comes down, you have a 29-homer outfielder with room to grow; if it stays where it is, he's a productive power bat who will frustrate you every time he expands.

reports.name: Kade Anderson
reports.published_report: A 1.1 ERA and a 0.6 WHIP at Double-A aren't numbers that need context — they're the argument. Anderson has struck out 135 batters against 13 walks across 93.3 innings at AA this season, and the command profile translates cleanly: a BB/9 of 2.0 in MLB terms, well below the 3.2 figure where most pitchers land, with a K-BB% that comes out to 21.9% against an average of 13.5%. The whole thing hinges on whether the stuff backs up the control at the highest level, because a left-hander this young who misses this many bats while almost never missing the zone has no obvious developmental ceiling short of a frontline starter. If the stuff softens in the jump, he's still a useful mid-rotation arm, but nothing in this line suggests you should expect softening.

reports.name: Theo Gillen
reports.published_report: The .419 OBP across AA & A+ is what grabs you, but the tension in Theo Gillen's profile is whether the contact quality survives MLB pitching. A .382 BABIP inflating a .315 average is the honest concern, yet a 14% walk rate and 22 home runs across AA & A+ in 533 plate appearances tell you this isn't someone simply riding balls in play — there's genuine strike-zone control and developing power underneath the batting average. The MLB-equivalent translation does knock the strikeout rate above league average and the power back toward ordinary, which is exactly what you'd expect from a 20-year-old still moving through the system, and the 44 stolen bases add a real dimension that survives level changes better than hit tools do. If the walk rate holds and the strikeout rate doesn't balloon further, he's a low-end everyday right fielder; if the contact regresses and the BABIP corrects hard, you're looking at a useful bench bat with speed.

A 10.0% strikeout rate is genuinely rare, and the 12.6% whiff rate backs it up, but the 2.3% barrel rate and 87.6 mph average exit velocity show you the ceiling — he's not manufacturing extra-base hits, he's manufacturing outs-avoided. The projection's .274/.318/.398 line across 607 PA is coherent with that shape: a guy who hits for average, chips in 13 steals, and gives you modest power that never becomes a real weapon. Everything holds if the contact quality stays consistent; if he runs into a stretch where pitchers can keep the ball off the barrel and his 4.9% walk rate offers no cushion, there's not much underneath.

reports.name: Carter Jensen
reports.published_report: The exit velo and the strikeout rate are telling completely different stories. Jensen hits the ball hard, 91.3 mph average exit velocity, a 12.0% barrel rate, 44.7% hard-hit, but a 28.0% K% drags the xBA down to .215, which is how you get loud contact with quiet batting averages. The saving grace is that his 23.9% chase rate ranks in the 86th percentile, meaning the strikeouts come from swinging and missing at strikes rather than fishing outside the zone, and an 11.1% walk rate suggests the plate discipline foundation is sturdy enough that 25 projected home runs can carry the line. If the whiff rate tightens even modestly, this profile becomes a plus everyday catcher; if it doesn't, he's a .233/.319/.451 guy who earns his roster spot with the pop and glove and not much else.

reports.name: Kody Clemens

The projection at 28 home runs over 584 plate appearances treats that contact quality as real, and the shape of the Statcast profile, barrels at 11.6%, hard contact in the 80th percentile, makes the power case believable even if the .302 OBP keeps the ceiling capped. Walk rate of 6.9% is where this profile gets uncomfortable, because if pitchers learn to exploit the 32.3% chase rate more aggressively, the power numbers erode before the on-base numbers can rescue him. reports.name: Bryce Miller
reports.published_report: The 35.0% chase rate is the engine — when hitters won't lay off his stuff out of the zone, the rest of the profile doesn't need to be elite. His 32.9% hard-hit rate allowed sits in the upper tier of the league, which is the tension: he generates chases at a level most starters envy, yet when contact does happen it's harder than you'd expect given a 2516 rpm fastball spin that should be producing more weak fly balls. The xERA of 3.69 says he's pitching better than a 4.18 ERA implies, and if the hard-hit rate normalizes downward, the gap closes fast toward something resembling a solid mid-rotation innings eater. The profile hinges on that chase rate holding; if hitters adjust and make him live in the zone, the whiff rate at 25.5% isn't loud enough to carry him.

reports.name: Leo De Vries
reports.published_report: The .290/.378/.458 line at AA is legitimate production for a 19-year-old, but the translation is where you feel the ceiling close in. His AA ISO of .168 becomes .135 at the MLB equivalent, and with the MLB average sitting at .150, the power that looks live in Double-A thins to fringe when the level adjusts. What holds up better is the discipline: 49 walks against 91 strikeouts across 428 PA translates to a 9.5% walk rate, and where the MLB average is 8.5%, that's a skill that travels. De Vries is either a solid-contact shortstop who develops enough gap power to hold a lineup spot, or a bench bat who hits for average and walks enough to stay on a roster when the ISO doesn't follow.

reports.name: Angel Genao
reports.published_report: The contact-and-patience combo is what makes this profile hum. Across AAA & AA in 2026, Genao is hitting .300/.401/.474 through 419 plate appearances, with 60 walks against just 68 strikeouts — a discipline profile that translates to an 11.5 BB% and a K% sitting below league average at the MLB level. The power is the open question: his .174 ISO in the minors translates to .141 at the MLB equivalent, a tick below average, which means if he doesn't add loft or pull-side juice, he becomes a shortstop who gets on base rather than one who damages you. If the hit tool holds and the walks travel, he grows into a low-end everyday regular; if the power translation stays thin, what's left is a bench bat who can still take a walk.

reports.name: A.J. Ewing
reports.published_report: The speed is the loudest thing in the profile, and 26 projected stolen bases on a .327 OBP is a real tension. At 29.5 ft/s Ewing is among the fastest players in baseball, and the 91st-percentile OAA says the speed plays in the field too, but the bat is what keeps this from being a simple story. A 25.1% strikeout rate with a .383 projected SLG doesn't leave much room for the offense to carry itself on contact alone, even though the 26.2% chase rate is a genuine positive and the xBA of .259 suggests the contact he does make plays up. If the strikeout rate stays where it is and the power doesn't grow, he's a high-end bench piece or a platoon-dependent regular; if the contact sharpens even modestly, the speed turns a fringy offensive profile into something an everyday lineup can build around.

reports.name: Zack Gelof
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile here is two guys arguing with each other. Gelof's chase rate sits at 24.7%, genuinely elite plate discipline at the point of contact selection, yet a 28.9% whiff rate and 25.2% K% drag the overall contact picture well below league average, and the .228 xBA reflects it honestly. The raw power metrics are real enough, 9.7% barrel rate, 42.3% hard-hit rate, 89.5 mph average exit velocity, but they feed a .416 xSLG, which is middling, because the contact itself is sparse enough to suppress the counting. Pair that with 28.8 ft/s sprint speed and he's a threat on the bases when he gets there, and the projection's 15 steals in 433 PA reflect that; the question is whether a .312 OBP gives him enough chances for the speed to matter. If the whiff rate drops even modestly, this is a solid second-division regular; if it doesn't, he's a power-speed profile whose contact floor keeps the OPS near the projection's .762 and the lineup role tenuous.

If the power plays, he's a platoon bat who can hurt righties; if the strikeout rate creeps further, he's a depth piece waiting on the next roster crunch.

The projection's .267/.361/.459 line in 489 plate appearances is believable given the raw power, but it hinges entirely on whether he can tighten contact without sacrificing the patient approach that makes him dangerous in the first place. reports.name: Termarr Johnson
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the loudest thing in this profile, and also the most complicated. At AAA in 2026, Termarr Johnson has drawn 68 walks against 101 strikeouts across 406 plate appearances, and that 17% walk rate translates to 13.1% at the MLB level, where most hitters sit around 8.5%. The power, though, is a different story: his .120 ISO at AAA translates to .114 in the majors, well short of the .150 MLB average, and a .199 average sitting on a .259 BABIP suggests the contact isn't beating defenders when it lands. The 24 stolen bases at AAA matter here, because if the legs can manufacture value that the bat isn't yet providing, the floor stays livable, but everything hinges on whether the contact quality catches up enough to make opposing pitchers respect the plate discipline instead of just pitching around it. Right now the ceiling is a bench or platoon bat, and the floor is the same.

reports.name: Jesús Luzardo

His 31.9% whiff rate and 33.7% chase rate explain why hitters aren't squaring him up; the 5.9% barrel rate and 33.2% hard-hit rate are what you'd expect from a pitcher generating that much swing-and-miss. The one lever that keeps this from being a totally clean profile is the 7.2% walk rate, which sits comfortably above the elite tier and is what separates him from true top-of-rotation aces when command wavers. If 179.7 innings of this holds in Philadelphia, you're looking at a genuine Cy Young conversation; if the walks climb and the health doesn't cooperate, the floor is still a mid-rotation arm who misses a lot of bats.

reports.name: Taj Bradley
reports.published_report: The strikeouts and the fastball point one direction; the contact quality points the other. Bradley punches out 27.3% of hitters, a genuinely upper-tier rate, and his 97.2 mph heater backs up why, yet the hard-hit rate sits at 45.2% with a barrel rate of 9.3%, both landing at the bottom of the league. That collision traces back to a 10.3% walk rate paired with a chase rate of just 28.3%: when hitters lay off his stuff, they force him into the zone, and when they connect there, they connect hard. His xERA of 3.99 running above the projected 3.83 ERA is a quiet warning that the underlying shape isn't quite backing the number, and if the walk and contact problems hold, the gap closes badly.

reports.name: Angel Martínez
reports.published_report:

reports.name: Zach Ehrhard
reports.published_report: The .401 OBP at AAA is doing real work here, but the translation is the part that deflates the profile. Across 621 plate appearances in AAA, Zach Ehrhard is hitting .290 with 93 walks, 20 home runs, and 27 stolen bases, a legitimately complete stat line for the level. The problem is that the ISO translates to .145 in an MLB equivalent, right at league average, and the K% lands at 22.1% while the MLB average sits at 22.0%, meaning the strikeout discipline that looks like a strength at AAA essentially disappears in translation. The walk rate holds at 12.5% translated, a number that would play in any big-league lineup, so there's a real skill underneath, but if the power doesn't add a tick in the jump, what you're left with is a high-OBP center fielder without the bat to carry a lineup spot.

The power gets him to 19 projected home runs and keeps him useful; the contact floor keeps him somewhere between a second-division regular and a DH who needs a platoon partner. reports.name: Brady Ebel

The power is nowhere close: his .154 ISO across A+ & A translates to .108 equivalent, well short of the MLB mean, and if the bat speed or loft don't develop, you're looking at a glove-and-patience shortstop who maxes out as a bench piece. Forty stolen bases across A+ & A give the profile another dimension, and the ceiling hinges entirely on whether in-game pop catches up to the plate discipline that's already here.

The tension is the strikeout rate, a 32.4% K% that lands at the 3rd percentile, meaning his .239 xBA will stay ugly no matter what happens; the .236 projected AVG is the cost of admission, not a correction waiting to happen. What saves it is a 14.4% BB% that keeps the OBP at .352 and the .365 xwOBA at the 92nd percentile, because he genuinely earns his walks rather than getting walked around trouble. At 33, with full playing time and that contact-quality floor, the projection resolves cleanly: a high-strikeout, high-walk, high-damage DH who doesn't need the batting average to matter.

reports.name: Bryce Harper
reports.published_report: The .385 xwOBA is the whole argument: it's 98th percentile, and it's built almost entirely on discipline rather than raw contact quality. His 15.9% walk rate sits at the 97th percentile while his average exit velocity and hard-hit rate are solidly ordinary, which means the production is coming from his ability to force favorable counts and make pitchers work — not from elite bat-to-ball or loud contact. The 30.4% whiff rate is a real tension in the profile; if pitchers find a way to limit his walks, the strikeouts become load-bearing in a bad way. But at 693 projected plate appearances with a .384 OBP, the floor here is a high-end regular whose on-base skills age better than speed or power.

reports.name: Cam Cauley
reports.published_report: The stolen base number is the loudest thing on this card: 36 at AAA across 416 plate appearances, and that's the engine the whole profile runs on. His bat translates to a 10.7 BB% at the MLB level, which is meaningfully above what most big-league hitters draw, while the ISO translation lands at .147, essentially a league-average power mark that won't carry him on its own. What keeps him interesting is the 53 walks against 86 strikeouts at AAA, a discipline profile that travels, and a shortstop who can run like that has a real floor even if the bat plateaus. If the speed holds and the on-base rate translates, he's a useful bench piece who can spell a starter and steal a game; if the contact erodes against better velocity, you're left with a pinch-runner and defensive sub at a premium position.

reports.name: Rafael Devers
reports.published_report: The gap between his .473 xSLG and .238 xBA is the whole Devers profile in two numbers: elite raw power, contact that bleeds enough outs to keep the batting average ordinary. At 93.0 mph average exit velocity and a 51.6% hard-hit rate, the damage when he connects is genuine, and a 12.5% barrel rate puts him in the conversation with the game's best pure hitters. The 25.4% strikeout rate is the dependency — it's what separates a .258/.340/.525 line from something more imposing, and if the whiff rate climbs in San Francisco's bigger park, the power numbers absorb the hit before the walk rate (10.9%) can compensate. He's a middle-of-the-order bat who produces more than his average suggests, and that's exactly what the projection reflects.

reports.name: Heriberto Hernández
reports.published_report: The power is legitimate and the Statcast profile keeps proving it: a 13.1% barrel rate and .478 xSLG both land in the upper tier of the league, and a 24.0% chase rate says he's selective enough to make contact matter when he squares it up. The problem is a 32.9% whiff rate that undercuts the whole thing, keeping his xBA at .247 even as the quality-of-contact numbers scream louder. The projection lands at 25 home runs over 500 PA with a .765 OPS, which is a usable outfielder, but the gap between that xSLG and his actual production is a contact question that won't resolve itself. Pull the whiff rate down and the power translates into a genuine everyday player; leave it where it sits and he's a lineup filler who hits the ball very hard in bursts.

His xwOBA sits at .342 and his BB% of 11.4% puts him well clear of the league norm, but the exit velocity and hard-hit rate are both right around league average, so the plate discipline is doing more lifting than the bat speed. The projection's .781 OPS over 474 PA reflects that mix honestly: a patient hitter who gets on base at a .354 clip but probably profiles as a solid-average third baseman rather than a power threat, with 13 projected home runs carrying the ceiling at Coors. reports.name: Jackson Kent
reports.published_report: The walk rate is doing a lot of work here, and it's holding up. Across AAA & AA this season, 30 walks in 94.4 innings translates to a BB/9 of 3.1 at the MLB equivalent, virtually identical to the 3.2 pitchers run on average, and the WHIP of 1.1 is the spine of a 3.7 ERA that grades out cleanly against the competition. The K-BB% of 20% across those levels translates to 14.5% in MLB terms, a tick above the league mean, which means the profile isn't built on strikeouts he doesn't quite own, his 10.0 K/9 in the minors comes back to 8.6 in translation, it's built on not giving hitters free passes. If the command holds in full-time big-league exposure, he's a multi-inning reliever with a real job; if it slips, 105 strikeouts don't leave enough margin to survive, and you're looking at a depth arm filling innings when someone goes down.

At AAA in 2026, Culpepper is hitting .271/.367/.478 across 343 plate appearances, with 14 home runs and 17 stolen bases, while striking out just 18% of the time. The translation tightens things up some — ISO drops to .16 at the MLB level, strikeouts tick up to 20.7%, but the walk rate translates to 9.8% against a MLB average that sits at 8.5%, and the contact profile holds enough shape to believe the hit tool carries. The ceiling here is a bench or platoon bat at short, which is genuinely useful, and the floor is organizational depth; what determines which end he lands on is whether the power holds even slightly against big-league arms, because the .16 ISO equivalent doesn't leave much margin.

reports.name: Robert Moore
reports.published_report: The contact rate is doing real work here, and not in the way you'd hope. A .219 BABIP over 311 AAA plate appearances is going to depress a batting line regardless of what else is happening, and what else is happening is legitimately interesting: 15 home runs, a .243 ISO, 33 walks against only 45 strikeouts. That contact-to-power shape translates to an 18.1% strikeout rate and .178 ISO against big-league pitching, both above the MLB mean in their respective directions, which means the discipline and the pop survive the level jump even if the average doesn't fully recover. The whole profile hinges on whether that BABIP is a ball-in-play luck crater or a signal that his hit tool is genuinely thin, because if it's the latter the .228 average at AAA becomes something closer to .200 in the majors and the on-base number collapses with it. Either a useful bench bat with real pop, or a guy who can't make enough contact to stay on a roster despite doing almost everything else right.

reports.name: Nathan Flewelling
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the most interesting thing in this profile, and it might also be the most misleading part. At A+ across 486 plate appearances, Flewelling has drawn 71 walks against 132 strikeouts, a 15% walk rate that translates to roughly 11% at the MLB level, a figure meaningfully ahead of where MLB hitters sit on average, but his 27% strikeout rate at A+ becomes something closer to 30.5% when you run it through the level adjustment, and that's a hard number to build a catcher's career around. The .208 ISO at A+ is loud for a 19-year-old at that level, yet it softens to about .144 in MLB-equivalent terms, which lands right at the league-average power band, meaning the profile that looks like a power-and-patience bat in High-A looks more like a fringe regular once you translate it. Everything here hinges on whether the strikeout rate bends as he climbs; if it doesn't, what's left is a bench catcher with acceptable plate discipline and middling pop.

reports.name: Will Warren
reports.published_report: The ERA looks palatable; the contact profile is not. Warren's 44.4% hard-hit rate and 90.9 mph average exit velocity sit at the very bottom of the leaderboard, and the .322 xwOBA with a 4.40 xERA is the truer picture of what hitters do when they connect. The saving grace is 2541 rpm on the fastball, elite spin that keeps strikeout and walk rates near average and presumably generates the weak swings when it works, but it isn't suppressing hard contact at a rate that makes a rotation spot comfortable. If the spin keeps missing bats and the hard contact stays manageable over a full season, he's a back-end starter who earns that 3.91 ERA projection; if it doesn't, the underlying numbers say 4.40 is closer to right, and you're looking at a long-relief arm getting stretched.

reports.name: Ty Johnson

reports.name: Foster Griffin
reports.published_report:
The ERA projection says front-of-rotation. The Statcast profile says something closer to survival.

Griffin's 3.68 ERA and 16 projected wins are built almost entirely on a walk rate that sits at 6.5%, which is genuinely elite control for a starter. But a 4.33 xERA and a 23.1% whiff rate tell you the strikeouts aren't coming at a rate that can cover mistakes, and 91.5 mph on the fastball with spin at 2089 rpm puts him near the bottom of the league in both. The whole profile hinges on contact management, meaning if hitters start squaring him up more consistently than that 8.5% barrel rate currently shows, there's not enough swing-and-miss to compensate. What you get if it holds is a back-end starter who earns his innings through command and keeps quality starts piling up; what you get if it doesn't is a swiftly exposed replacement-level arm.

reports.name: Andrés Giménez
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile here is about as bleak as it gets for a guy still drawing everyday reps: 85.4 mph average exit velocity at the 4th percentile, a 3.3% barrel rate, 24.7% hard-hit rate, and a chase rate of 43.8% that sits at the 2nd percentile leaguewide. Those contact-quality numbers explain the .272 xwOBA cleanly, no translation needed. The 3.3% walk rate is similarly near the bottom of the sport, so there's no patient approach bailing out the weak contact. What keeps Giménez from being a pure roster problem is 27.8 ft/s sprint speed and elite defense at second, with the fielding OAA percentile at 99th, which means his floor is a high-end glove who steals 21 bases in projection and costs you nothing in the field. If the bat stays this suppressed, he's a defensive specialist you're overplaying, and the .649 projected OPS across 519 plate appearances is the honest ceiling until he does something about the zone management.

Across AA & A+, Kepley has drawn 120 walks against just 89 strikeouts in 595 plate appearances, a 20% walk rate that translates to 14.7% at the MLB level, well above the league norm of 8.5%. The .422 OBP stands on a foundation the contact backs up, a 15% strikeout rate that would play below league average at the big-league level, but the ISO translates to .12, a tick below MLB average, and 70 stolen bases tell you he's betting his value on getting on base rather than doing damage. If the plate discipline holds in Triple-A and the speed stays viable, there's a legitimate bench piece here; if the walks compress under better pitching and the power doesn't grow, what's left is a .243 hitter with nothing to carry him.

reports.name: Troy Melton
reports.published_report: The gap between a 2.67 ERA projection and a 3.74 xERA is the whole conversation with Melton. His 32.4% chase rate is legitimate, putting him in the upper third of the league on that metric, but a 20.0% strikeout rate means he's not finishing those chases at anything like an elite clip. What he is, then, is a contact manager who relies on suppressing barrels at 6.2% rather than missing bats, and that kind of pitcher lives and dies by strand rate and sequencing luck. If the ERA drifts toward the xERA over a full season, you're looking at a back-end starter who logs innings competently; if the chase rate and barrel suppression hold together, he can outperform his stuff in ways that look fluky until they don't.

reports.name: Tristan Peters
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile is mostly below average except for two things that point in opposite directions. His sprint speed at 28.7 ft/s grades elite, and his fielding OAA sits at the 97th percentile. The bat, though, is soft: 87.4 mph average exit velocity and a 33.8% hard-hit rate both check in around the 22nd percentile, and his .316 xwOBA reflects a hitter who makes enough contact to survive but not enough damage to carry a lineup spot. ValuCast's projection of .271/.342/.448 across 499 PA probably leans on that contact rate holding and the speed creating value the batted-ball data can't fully capture. If his legs cool or the park context stops being kind, you're left with a glove-first outfielder whose bat grades as a liability rather than a complement.

That's a lefty who commands the zone well enough that the strikeout volume, 143 across 106.6 innings, doesn't feel like a walk-rate trade-off. reports.name: Santiago Suarez
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the whole profile. At AA, 21 walks across 126 innings translates to a 2.1 BB/9 in MLB-equivalent terms, well below the 3.2 mark most pitchers run at that level, and that gap is wide enough to carry a guy whose 99 strikeouts don't translate to missing bats up top — the MLB-equivalent K/9 comes out at 6.6, well short of the 8.6 average. The control is real enough to keep him viable, but the ceiling math doesn't clear the bar: even with pinpoint command, a pitcher who misses few bats and works toward the middle of the zone doesn't have the margin for error a backend starter needs. Suarez is a depth arm if it stays together, and a depth arm if something slips.

reports.name: Brady House
reports.published_report: The xBA-to-actual-BA gap is the whole argument here. House is hitting .240 in the projection but his xBA sits at .269, and a 47.9% hard-hit rate puts him in the top quarter of the league at making loud contact. The problem is a 33.9% chase rate and 30.0% whiff rate that keep the ball out of play often enough to suppress what his power profile actually suggests, because an xSLG of .446 against a current projected .395 SLG is meaningful distance. If he ever quiets the zone-expansion habit, the contact quality is already there to push him toward a solid everyday corner; if he doesn't, a .696 OPS third baseman on a rebuilding Washington club is exactly the ceiling.

reports.name: Evan Carter
reports.published_report:
The Statcast profile reads like two different players stapled together. His 20.8% chase rate sits at the 96th percentile, genuine elite zone discipline, and his 10.8% walk rate is comfortably above average. Then you look at what happens once he swings: a .199 xBA, a 29.1% whiff rate, contact quality in the bottom handful of the league.

The problem is that the walks can't carry him if the contact is this soft. A .279 xwOBA translates to a hitter who is actively hurting a lineup, and the projection, across 458 PA, reflects exactly that: a .196/.293/.323 line where the 17 stolen bases are doing the most meaningful offensive work. He sticks in center if the glove is what the 95th-percentile OAA suggests, but unless the whiff rate comes down or the exit velocity climbs off 87.8 mph, he's a defensive specialist with a pretty walk rate and not much else.

reports.name: Blake Mitchell
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the loudest thing on this card, and it's also the problem. At A+ in 2026, Blake Mitchell has drawn 113 walks in 511 plate appearances, a 22% clip that sits at the 99th percentile of his pool, and he's added 27 stolen bases and 23 home runs on top of it, a legitimately unusual combination for a catcher at 21. But the .234 average against a .346 BABIP tells you the strikeouts aren't disappearing, and when that contact rate translates to an MLB-equivalent 36.8% K%, what survives the jump is a 15.4% walk rate propped up against average power at .152 ISO. The whole profile hinges on whether the discipline holds as pitchers locate better, because if the strikeouts climb and the walks compress even modestly, the .234 average becomes the story rather than the footnote. If it works, he's a patient, borderline-average offensive catcher who runs; if it doesn't, the bench is the ceiling.

reports.name: Dylan Dreiling
reports.published_report: The .312 average and .896 OPS at AA are loud, and they should be — 538 plate appearances is a real season, not a hot week. What complicates the read is the translation: the power that looks like a carrying tool at AA (.204 ISO, 22 home runs) softens to a .154 MLB equivalent, and the strikeout rate ticks up to 23.1% against a game where the average hitter strikes out 22.0% of the time. The walk rate translates cleanly at 9.0%, but that's a support beam, not a foundation. If the power holds any of its AA shape in the upper levels, Dreiling is a useful left-handed center fielder who can spell an everyday player and take a walk; if the ISO just melts on contact with better arms, what's left is a high-BABIP profile that won't survive the jump.

reports.name: Griffin Jax
reports.published_report: The chase rate is elite and the spin is genuinely rare, but the underlying contact profile undercuts both. Jax runs a 35.2% chase rate and 30.1% whiff rate that any reliever would covet, yet his xwOBA sits at .322 and his xERA at 4.39, meaning when hitters do make contact they're doing real damage, a 9.2% barrel rate that lands in the bottom fifth of the league. The projection pencils him in at 3.78 ERA over 114.9 innings, a number that assumes the surface results hold, and the whole read hinges on whether he can suppress hard contact better than his Statcast profile suggests he currently does. If he can't, the 4.39 xERA is closer to who he is: a high-chase, high-spin arm whose swing-and-miss tools make him useful out of Tampa's bullpen even as a full starter's workload remains a stretch.

reports.name: Matthew Etzel
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the loudest thing in this profile, and it's also the thing that exposes the ceiling problem. Across 493 plate appearances at AAA, Etzel is drawing walks at a 13% clip, which translates to an 11.2% MLB-equivalent rate while the league sits at 8.5%, and the .189 ISO at AAA suggests real enough pull-side thump to force pitchers into that zone. The trouble is the contact: a .243 average against a .296 BABIP means he isn't getting beaten on balls in play, he's just not hitting them hard enough often enough, and the MLB-equivalent strikeout rate of 25.3% will play worse against big-league stuff than it does now. If the power holds in translation, you've got a patient lefty bat who can work counts and punish mistakes off the bench; if the strikeouts creep and the ISO shrinks, what's left is a quadruple-A hitter who takes walks in an empty at-bat.

reports.name: Sandy Alcantara
reports.published_report: 97.5 mph on the fastball but a 17.3% strikeout rate — that's the whole tension in Alcantara's profile right now. The velocity is genuine, the miss rate isn't keeping up with it, and a 21.0% whiff rate explains why: he's getting contact managed rather than overmatched, living on a 5.8% barrel rate and a 6.7% walk rate that keeps rallies from compounding. The projection reads as a durable mid-rotation workhorse who earns his value through volume and contact suppression, not a strikeout-driven ace, and the xERA of 3.90 says that's probably right. If the whiff rate climbs back toward what that fastball should generate, the ERA improves and the floor gets higher; if it stays flat, he's still useful for 216.6 innings of league-average-ish run prevention, which isn't nothing on a Miami staff.

reports.name: Miguel Ullola
reports.published_report: The strikeouts are loud, the walks are a problem, and that gap is basically the whole profile. Across 66.3 innings at AAA in 2026, Ullola is missing bats at a 12.2 K/9 clip while issuing 42 walks, and when you translate that to MLB context the walk rate comes out to 4.8 — more than a run and a half above what MLB starters typically allow. The K-BB% sits at 17% in the raw AAA line, which ranks 76th percentile in the pitcher pool, but that number flatters him a little: MLB-equivalent, it translates to 13.6%, nearly indistinguishable from the 13.5% MLB average, meaning the swing-and-miss checks out across the sample but the command leaks are eating most of the gains. If the zone-attack sharpens, there's a back-end piece somewhere in here; if it doesn't, 90 strikeouts in the minors becomes organizational depth.

reports.name: JT Quinn
reports.published_report: The 3.4 ERA and 1.2 WHIP across AA & A+ paint a controlled, contact-suppressing arm, and the 89th-percentile WHIP among starters with meaningful innings backs the picture up. The translation is the complication: his 10.0 K/9 softens to 7.8 against big-league hitters, a rate that sits below what the average MLB starter posts, and his walk rate edges from manageable to slightly above the mean in the same conversion. What he has is command feel and a contact-suppression profile that's held over 116.7 innings; what he lacks is a strikeout weapon that survives the climb. Everything hinges on whether the control is real enough to carry him as a starter when the strikeout gap widens — if it is, he works as a back-end rotation piece; if it isn't, he's a depth arm in bulk innings.

reports.name: Jacob Melton
reports.published_report: Twenty-six stolen bases in 186 AAA plate appearances is the loudest thing in this profile, and it's almost the only thing that survives translation. Melton's .222 ISO at AAA looks like real pull-side power, but it deflates to .163 against MLB arms, about where league average sits, and the 33% strikeout rate at AAA becomes 28.7% in the majors, well above the 22.0% league norm. The hit tool isn't helping: a .359 BABIP propping a .253 AAA average is the kind of foundation that collapses the moment the bat-to-ball problem gets exposed at the next level. If the speed plays in center and the strikeout rate bends down, he's a useful bench piece; if it doesn't, the floor is a roster filler who never sticks.

reports.name: Bryce Rainer

Across A+ & A in 2026, Bryce Rainer has hit 19 home runs with 69 walks in 478 plate appearances, and the walk rate translates to a respectable 10.8% MLB-equivalent — the plate patience is genuine, the power shapes into something. But he has also struck out 171 times, and that 36% rate at this level translates to 38.3% against big-league pitching, well past the point where carrying an everyday shortstop becomes comfortable. The ISO sits at .205 across A+ & A, and the raw production looks loud, but a .396 BABIP is doing real work to prop the average up, and when that normalizes the contact problem gets harder to paper over. If the strikeouts compress as he climbs, there's a second-division regular hiding in the profile; if they don't, what remains is a bench bat with a good eye and fringe power.
